summary: Observes that different applications need different amounts of session continuity or IP address reachability when a device moves, yet networks treat them all alike, as noted in RFC 7333. It proposes letting applications influence the mobility service on a per-socket basis and suggests extensions to the networking stack API for this.

plainLanguage.summary: Some trips need your home address to follow you and some do not. This lets each program tell the network how much help it needs when you move.

questions: ip address reachability for mobile hosts
types of ip addresses for mobile hosts
subtitle: Let mobile apps request exactly the IP stability they need.

tldr.problem: Mobile hosts running different applications have different needs for session continuity and IP address stability, yet networks provide the same service to all, causing inefficiency.
tldr.mechanism: Applications can request one of four IP address types (Fixed, Session-Lasting, Nonpersistent, or Graceful-Replacement) when opening a socket, and the network stack provides the appropriate service.
tldr.outcome: Applications get the mobility service they need without unnecessary overhead, saving network resources and reducing latency for applications that do not require full mobility support.

today: RFC 8653 is an Informational document that proposes a concept and API extensions for networks to support. Adoption by mobile operators and devices is not widespread; the feature remains a design proposal rather than a deployed protocol.

sections.title: The Problem with One-Size-Fits-All Mobility
sections.content:
Mobile hosts using protocols like Mobile IP are designed to maintain both session continuity (the same IP address during an ongoing connection) and IP address reachability (a persistent IP address that can be published in DNS or reached for incoming connections). However, not every application needs both. A mobile web server needs a fixed IP address so clients can find it, but a web browser client does not; a text messaging app does not need either. When Mobile IP provides these expensive services to every application on every host, it incurs unnecessary transmission latency, network resource consumption, and infrastructure costs.

RFC 7333 described these inefficiencies. This RFC proposes letting applications indicate their requirements on a per-socket basis, so the network provides only the services that are actually needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine everyone in a neighborhood gets premium express mail service, even if they just need regular delivery. It is wasteful. This lets each person request the service they actually need.

sections.title: Four Types of IP Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC defines four address types based on how long they remain valid and whether they survive network handovers:

Fixed IP address: Valid indefinitely, even across handovers and disconnections. Required for applications like web servers that need a published address or long-running SSH sessions.

Session-Lasting IP address: Valid for the lifetime of the socket(s) that requested it, surviving handovers but not indefinite disconnection. Suits applications like web browsers that need continuity during use but do not need a permanent address.

Nonpersistent IP address: Lost on handover; no session continuity or address reachability. Appropriate for very brief transactions like DNS queries or instant messages.

Graceful-Replacement IP address: A middle ground: the network guarantees a transition period where both the old and new IP prefix are valid, allowing applications time to migrate. Useful for streaming clients with buffering capabilities that can tolerate brief interruptions.
sections.plainLanguage: Fixed is like owning a house with a permanent address. Session-Lasting is like renting a temporary apartment that is yours during your stay. Nonpersistent is like asking a stranger for directions; you get an answer but not a permanent relationship. Graceful-Replacement is like getting a forwarding address before you move.

sections.title: How Applications Request a Service Type
sections.content:
Applications indicate their requirements at socket creation time using a new socket option (the RFC suggests extending IPV6_ADDR_PREFERENCE from RFC 5014 or creating a new function like setsc() to SetServiceContinuity()). The local IP stack maintains a pool of available IP address types, provided by the network through prior negotiation. When an application requests an address type, the stack either assigns an existing one from that pool or contacts the network to request a new IP prefix with the desired properties. If successful, the application receives the address and binds it to the socket. If the operation fails, the socket request returns an error.

The granularity is per-socket, so a single application can use different address types for different connections based on what each connection needs.
sections.plainLanguage: When you open a socket, you can ask for the kind of address you need. The stack either gives you one it already has or asks the network for a new one. You get what you asked for, or an error if it is not available.

sections.title: Compatibility with Existing Systems
sections.content:
Legacy applications that do not use the new API continue to work with traditional behavior: the network assigns an address type based on its own policy or defaults, likely a Fixed or Session-Lasting address to be safe. New IP stacks must support both the old API and the new one. Networks may or may not support the feature; if a modern app tries to request a specific address type on a legacy network, the API returns an error and the app can fall back to traditional behavior.

The RFC also notes that if an application uses both the old RFC 5014 flags (for selecting address prefixes like home addresses or temporary addresses) and the new On-Demand flags simultaneously, the new flags take precedence and the old ones are ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Old apps keep working the old way. New apps can ask for what they need, but if the network does not support it, they get an error and can try the old way instead.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Concerns
sections.content:
Malicious applications could exploit this feature to request expensive services (like Fixed IP addresses) to exhaust network resources or generate unexpected billing for the subscriber. Mobile hosts that support On-Demand services should enforce authorization policies to ensure only legitimate applications can request costly address types.

The choice of address type can reveal information to passive observers about what an application is doing. To mitigate this, operators should vary which prefixes are associated with which address types over time, and applications should periodically request new addresses even when existing ones are available. Additionally, applications and the OS should rotate addresses regularly to limit IP-based tracking of user behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad app could ask for expensive services to cause problems. To stay safe, devices should check who is asking and also change addresses frequently to avoid being tracked.
